newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's fight with Bonn may prompt change-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Buba's fight with Bonn may prompt change-analysts.

text.p: An unusual public battle between Bonn and the Bundesbank, underlining the central bank's crusade for a strong European currency, may still force the government to alter plans, analysts said on Thursday.

"Currently one gets the impression that the government intends to push through its plans, but it will be critical to see if the coalition can hold together" in the face of the Bundesbank's categorical rejection of such steps, said Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.

At issue is Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to revalue German currency and gold reserves now, using some of the proceeds to shore up Germany's finances in order to qualify for Europe's currency union.

But the last-ditch effort, unveiled after Waigel's coalition partners flatly rejected a tax hike to plug the deficit, fell on stony ground at the central bank which saw Bonn's plan as interferance with Bundesbank independence and likely to compromise Germany's position in the runup to currency union.

Analysts reasoned the Bundesbank minced no words with Bonn for two reasons: first the Frankfurt bankers dislike government meddling, and second by uniting public opinion behind the central bank, Bonn might still be forced to back off.

"The statement was driven by their basic instincts," said Alison Cottrell, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London, adding "if the government decides to pull a fiscal fast one, the Bundesbank is going to complain very loudly."

Most troubling for the Bundesbank appears to be not the fact that gold will need to revalued but the timing of the announcement and the suggestion that some proceeds could be transferred to Bonn this year to fill government coffers.

"Waigel now looks like he has no principles, resorting to the same sort of creative accounting tricks that he had accused other nations, like Italy and France, of using," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.

But as German public opinion appears to rally behind the Bundesbank, still seen as the knight in shining armour fighting for a stable mark and later the euro, analysts feel the Kohl government's slim parliamentary majority might crumble.
"The government's position may be altered if the media potrays this as a real scandal," said Ros Lifton, economist at HSBC Markets in London.

The timing of the statement, coming just days before parliament is to vote on a change to the Bundesbank law which could force such a revaluation, was surely part of a plan to try and sway opinion, she added.
As the battle is sure to escalate, analysts worry that the Bundesbank's hardline stance, although fundamentally positive, could turn into a double-edged sword, rattling financial markets.

"The conflict will have consequences for the market, especially if it weighs on the mark which could refan inflationary pressures and force the Bundesbank to act quickly on raising rates at some point," Morgan Stanley's Fels said.
Traders agreed, saying German bond market losses were still limited compared which what could occur if markets sense the German government is really at odds with the Bundesbank.
"If the supports go, we could see a real bloodbath," Norman Beauchamp, trader at Co-Operative Bank in London said.
The brewing conflict also raises the question of whether some members of the Bundesbank, all no strangers to conflict with Bonn, might step down in protest.
"I would not rule it out that Tietmeyer could step down if the government sticks to its plans," Fels said.
But PaineWebber's Cottrell reasoned that any resignations could make the Bundesbank vulnerable, leaving Bonn to appoint a possibly less fervent advocate of a strong currency union to the position.

"Since Tietmeyer has gone through the whole process of preparing for currency union, he is going to see this through, sitting in Frankfurt and making their (the government's) lives very difficult," she said.
